content.text:
All seven plans are written to `docs/superpowers/plans/`.

## The set, in execution order

| # | Plan | Tasks | What it fixes |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **`daily-looks`** | 7 | Occasion taps read stored looks instead of firing an AI call. ~5× less AI spend, no 3s wait. |
| 2 | **`webp-cutouts`** | 3 | 1.84 MB per look → ~400 KB. |
| 3 | **`signed-url-cache`** | 3 | Stable URLs, so the browser can finally cache. |
| 4 | **`intent-first-entry`** | 4 | "What's today?" — one call, lazy per-occasion, weather-drift offer. |
| 5 | **`regenerate-quota`** | 4 | The paid-tier seam, with the daily drop never rationed. |
| 6 | **`cutout-backfill`** | 3 | Existing PNGs re-encoded via a one-off `sharp` script. |
| 7 | **`route-url-audit`** | 5 | `/today`, occasion in the URL, `/outfits/[id]`, manifest, revalidation. |

Every plan is TDD — failing test, watch it fail, minimal implementation — with real test code, not descriptions. Verification is in the iOS Simulator with the dev log open, per your new rule.

## Three things worth knowing

**Your old handoff note is now closed.** It said a transient *"Couldn't reach the stylist"* had been seen twice and the cause never captured. That was the 24-character name cap — fixed in PR #7. It wasn't transient; it fired whenever Haiku wrote a name one word too long.

**Plan 1 absorbs a pre-existing lint error.** `stylist.tsx:99` — "setState synchronously within an effect" — is in the exact effect Plan 1 rewrites, so it gets fixed there rather than as separate cleanup.

**The dependency chain is real, not bureaucratic.** Plan 4 reads and writes the daily set Plan 1 introduces; Plan 5 fills the `quota.ts` seam Plan 1 leaves; Plan 6 must run *after* Plan 2 or it runs twice; Plan 7 assumes persistence exists. Only 2 and 3 are independent — you could do those first if you want a quick visible win before the big one.

## Not in any plan

Three loose ends, recorded in the handoff so they don't resurface as mystery bugs:

- **iCloud is probably still creating the `" 2."` duplicates.** The gitignore stops them reaching git; it does *not* stop `tsc` typechecking them and breaking `npm run build` — which is what actually happened today. Worth checking whether that folder is synced.
- **Design-system findings** (off-ramp font sizes in three components) — pre-existing, needs its own `/impeccable audit`.
- **PR #6 has to merge before #7**, or none of this reaches `main`.

Want me to start executing Plan 1, or would you rather read the plans first?

# Executing Plans

## Overview

Load plan, review critically, execute all tasks, report when complete.

**Announce at start:** "I'm using the executing-plans skill to implement this plan."

**Note:** Tell your human partner that Superpowers works much better with access to subagents. The quality of its work will be significantly higher if run on a platform with subagent support (Claude Code, Codex CLI, Codex App, and Copilot CLI all qualify; see the per-platform tool refs in `../using-superpowers/references/`). If subagents are available, use superpowers:subagent-driven-development instead of this skill.

## The Process

### Step 1: Load and Review Plan
1. Read plan file
2. Review critically - identify any questions or concerns about the plan
3. If concerns: Raise them with your human partner before starting
4. If no concerns: Create todos for the plan items and proceed

### Step 2: Execute Tasks

For each task:
1. Mark as in_progress
2. Follow each step exactly (plan has bite-sized steps)
3. Run verifications as specified
4. Mark as completed

### Step 3: Complete Development

After all tasks complete and verified:
- Announce: "I'm using the finishing-a-development-branch skill to complete this work."
- **REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use superpowers:finishing-a-development-branch
- Follow that skill to verify tests, present options, execute choice

## When to Stop and Ask for Help

**STOP executing immediately when:**
- Hit a blocker (missing dependency, test fails, instruction unclear)
- Plan has critical gaps preventing starting
- You don't understand an instruction
- Verification fails repeatedly

**Ask for clarification rather than guessing.**

## When to Revisit Earlier Steps

**Return to Review (Step 1) when:**
- Partner updates the plan based on your feedback
- Fundamental approach needs rethinking

**Don't force through blockers** - stop and ask.

## Remember
- Review plan critically first
- Follow plan steps exactly
- Don't skip verifications
- Reference skills when plan says to
- Stop when blocked, don't guess
- Never start implementation on main/master branch without explicit user consent

## Integration

**Required workflow skills:**
- **superpowers:using-git-worktrees** - Ensures isolated workspace (creates one or verifies existing)
- **superpowers:writing-plans** - Creates the plan this skill executes
- **superpowers:finishing-a-development-branch** - Complete development after all tasks

input.content:
-- The daily drop (see CLAUDE.md "Decision 5"): looks are generated ONCE per
-- local day per occasion and then read back, not regenerated on every tap.
--
-- generated_on is the USER'S local date (lib/outfits/local-date.ts), never UTC.
-- look_index is the position within the day's set of three, so the order the
-- stylist chose survives a round trip.
alter table public.outfits
  add column if not exists generated_on date,
  add column if not exists look_index    smallint;

-- One row per (user, occasion, day, position). A regenerate deletes the day's
-- rows and re-inserts, so this also stops a double-submit writing six looks.
create unique index if not exists outfits_daily_unique
  on public.outfits (user_id, occasion, generated_on, look_index)
  where generated_on is not null;

-- The read path: "today's set for this occasion".
create index if not exists outfits_daily_lookup
  on public.outfits (user_id, occasion, generated_on);

On-device bg removal (free) · mini-model tagging (one-time per item) · text-only re-ranking · cache results.
The free tier must stay genuinely great — consumer apps die when the paywall hits before the magic moment.

### Decision 5: Looks are a daily drop, not a live generator
Fitcheck generates a user's looks **once per local day, per occasion**, and persists them to
`outfits` / `outfit_items` (`lib/outfits/`). Tapping an occasion READS the stored set; it does not call
the model. Only an explicit **Regenerate** spends an AI call on a day already answered.

- "Today" is the user's **local** date (`lib/outfits/local-date.ts`), never UTC — a UTC key rolls the
  drop over mid-evening for eastern users. A new local day generates a fresh set keyed on the new date;
  prior days' rows remain as history and are never read (`loadDailyLooks` filters on `generated_on`).
- If the closet changed under a stored set (an item was deleted), `reassembleLooks` returns null and the
  set is regenerated rather than rendered with a gap.
- `saveDailyLooks` is delete-then-insert, not upsert: a regenerate may return a different number of looks,
  and leftovers must not survive alongside the new set.
- This replaced a generator that re-ran on every occasion tap — ~5× the AI spend and a ~3s wait on every
  interaction. Because generation is once-a-day, latency work (streaming the model response) is
  deliberately NOT a priority; image weight and caching matter more, since a persisted look is re-opened
  all day.
- `lib/outfits/quota.ts` is the seam for a future paid tier (see the regenerate-quota plan).

# Finishing a Development Branch

## Overview

Guide completion of development work by presenting clear options and handling chosen workflow.

**Core principle:** Verify tests → Detect environment → Present options → Execute choice → Clean up.

**Announce at start:** "I'm using the finishing-a-development-branch skill to complete this work."

## The Process

### Step 1: Verify Tests

**Before presenting options, verify tests pass:**

```bash
# Run project's test suite
npm test / cargo test / pytest / go test ./...
```

**If tests fail:**
```
Tests failing (<N> failures). Must fix before completing:

[Show failures]

Cannot proceed with merge/PR until tests pass.
```

Stop. Don't proceed to Step 2.

**If tests pass:** Continue to Step 2.

### Step 2: Detect Environment

**Determine workspace state before presenting options:**

```bash
GIT_DIR=$(cd "$(git rev-parse --git-dir)" 2>/dev/null && pwd -P)
GIT_COMMON=$(cd "$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)" 2>/dev/null && pwd -P)
```

| `GIT_DIR != GIT_COMMON`, named branch | Standard 4 options | Provenance-based (see Step 6) |

```bash
git merge-base HEAD main 2>/dev/null || git merge-base HEAD master 2>/dev/null
```

```
3. Discard this work

Which option?
```

```bash
cd "$MAIN_ROOT"

# Merge first — verify success before removing anything
git checkout <base-branch>
git pull
git merge <feature-branch>

# Verify tests on merged result
<test command>

# Only after merge succeeds: cleanup worktree (Step 6), then delete branch
```

Then: Cleanup worktree (Step 6), then delete branch:

```bash

```

#### Option 2: Push and Create PR

```bash
# Push branch
git push -u origin <feature-branch>
```

**Do NOT clean up worktree** — user needs it alive to iterate on PR feedback.

#### Option 3: Keep As-Is

Report: "Keeping branch <name>. Worktree preserved at <path>."

**Don't cleanup worktree.**

#### Option 4: Discard

**Confirm first:**
```
This will permanently delete:
- Branch <name>
- All commits: <commit-list>
- Worktree at <path>

Type 'discard' to confirm.
```

Wait for exact confirmation.

If confirmed:
```bash
MAIN_ROOT=$(git -C "$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)/.." rev-parse --show-toplevel)
cd "$MAIN_ROOT"
```

Then: Cleanup worktree (Step 6), then force-delete branch:
```bash

```

### Step 6: Cleanup Workspace

**Only runs for Options 1 and 4.** Options 2 and 3 always preserve the worktree.

```bash
GIT_DIR=$(cd "$(git rev-parse --git-dir)" 2>/dev/null && pwd -P)
GIT_COMMON=$(cd "$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)" 2>/dev/null && pwd -P)
WORKTREE_PATH=$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)
```

**If `GIT_DIR == GIT_COMMON`:** Normal repo, no worktree to clean up. Done.

**If worktree path is under `.worktrees/` or `worktrees/`:** Superpowers created this worktree — we own cleanup.

```bash
MAIN_ROOT=$(git -C "$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)/.." rev-parse --show-toplevel)
cd "$MAIN_ROOT"
git worktree remove "$WORKTREE_PATH"
git worktree prune  # Self-healing: clean up any stale registrations
```

**Otherwise:** The host environment (harness) owns this workspace. Do NOT remove it. If your platform provides a workspace-exit tool, use it. Otherwise, leave the workspace in place.

| Option | Merge | Push | Keep Worktree | Cleanup Branch |
|--------|-------|------|---------------|----------------|
| 1. Merge locally | yes | - | - | yes |
| 2. Create PR | - | yes | yes | - |
| 3. Keep as-is | - | - | yes | - |
| 4. Discard | - | - | - | yes (force) |

## Common Mistakes

**Skipping test verification**
- **Problem:** Merge broken code, create failing PR
- **Fix:** Always verify tests before offering options

**Open-ended questions**
- **Problem:** "What should I do next?" is ambiguous
- **Fix:** Present exactly 4 structured options (or 3 for detached HEAD)

**Cleaning up worktree for Option 2**
- **Problem:** Remove worktree user needs for PR iteration
- **Fix:** Only cleanup for Options 1 and 4

**Deleting branch before removing worktree**
- **Problem:** `git branch -d` fails because worktree still references the branch
- **Fix:** Merge first, remove worktree, then delete branch

**Running git worktree remove from inside the worktree**
- **Problem:** Command fails silently when CWD is inside the worktree being removed
- **Fix:** Always `cd` to main repo root before `git worktree remove`

**Cleaning up harness-owned worktrees**
- **Problem:** Removing a worktree the harness created causes phantom state
- **Fix:** Only clean up worktrees under `.worktrees/` or `worktrees/`

**No confirmation for discard**
- **Problem:** Accidentally delete work
- **Fix:** Require typed "discard" confirmation

## Red Flags

**Never:**
- Proceed with failing tests
- Merge without verifying tests on result
- Delete work without confirmation
- Force-push without explicit request
- Remove a worktree before confirming merge success
- Clean up worktrees you didn't create (provenance check)
- Run `git worktree remove` from inside the worktree

**Always:**
- Verify tests before offering options
- Detect environment before presenting menu
- Present exactly 4 options (or 3 for detached HEAD)
- Get typed confirmation for Option 4
- Clean up worktree for Options 1 & 4 only
- `cd` to main repo root before worktree removal
- Run `git worktree prune` after removal

## The bug this fixes

Every occasion tap fired a full AI generation. `occasion` was a dependency of the generate effect in `stylist.tsx`, so tapping Everyday → Work → Weekend → Evening made **four Haiku calls** and waited ~3s each time. That is roughly 5× the AI spend and a live wait on every interaction — and it directly contradicts what the app is: a once-a-day styling ritual, not a live generator.

## The model (Decision 5)

Fitcheck now generates a user's looks **once per local day, per occasion**, and persists them to the `outfits` / `outfit_items` tables (which Plan 06 created but never used). Tapping an occasion READS the stored set. Only an explicit **Regenerate** spends an AI call on a day already answered.

- **"Today" is the user's local date** (`lib/outfits/local-date.ts`), never UTC — a UTC key would roll the drop over mid-evening for eastern users. A new local day generates a fresh set keyed on the new date; prior days' rows remain as history and are never read.
- **A closet edit under a stored set makes it stale** — `reassembleLooks` returns null and the set regenerates, rather than rendering a look with a hole in it.
- **`saveDailyLooks` is delete-then-insert**, not upsert: a regenerate may return a different number of looks, and leftovers must not survive alongside the new set.
- **`lib/outfits/quota.ts`** is a no-op seam so the future paid tier is a one-file change, not surgery.

## Verified end-to-end (iOS Simulator + browser, real Haiku)

| Behaviour | Result |
|---|---|
| Reload | reads DB, **no AI call** |
| Switch between stored occasions (×3) | zero new rows, **zero AI calls** |
| Tap an ungenerated occasion | generates once, then stored |
| Regenerate | replaces today's set with new IDs, exactly 3 rows |
| Date rollover (crossed midnight live) | fresh set keyed on the new local date |

The regenerate is a direct call, not an effect flag — a flag routed through the effect can still be in flight when the user switches occasion and would regenerate that one too.

## Checks

- **164 tests** (was 155; +9 TDD'd red-first across `local-date`, `reassemble`, and the regenerate control)
- `tsc --noEmit` clean · `npm run build` clean
- `npm run lint` — 5 errors / 8 warnings, **identical to baseline** (all pre-existing; the `setState-in-effect` warning on the generate effect is unchanged and deliberate — it shows the skeleton the instant inputs change)

## Migration

`20260722100000_outfits_daily.sql` — adds `generated_on` + `look_index` to `outfits`, a unique index on `(user_id, occasion, generated_on, look_index)`, and a daily-lookup index.

First of seven plans in `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-07-22-*.md`. The rest, in order: webp-cutouts → signed-url-cache → intent-first-entry → regenerate-quota → cutout-backfill → route-url-audit.

## The problem

`@imgly/background-removal` returns an **uncompressed PNG**, and today it went straight to Storage untouched — while the *original* photo (which users barely see) is carefully compressed to ≤500 KB. Measured on a real look: three cutouts at 540 / 714 / 588 KB — **1.84 MB per outfit**, re-downloaded on every view. The displayed image was larger than the JPEG original it came from.

## The fix

A new `lib/images/encode.ts` re-encodes the cutout to WebP on-device via canvas (WebP supports alpha, so transparency survives), with a PNG fallback whenever WebP is unavailable, unsupported, or simply not smaller. Storage path and content type follow the format actually produced, so WebP and legacy PNG cutouts coexist with no migration.

- **One pass at quality 0.85** — not lower, because the same blob is sent to Haiku for tagging and Anthropic's vision guidance warns that heavy compression hurts model accuracy.
- **Trust the result, not the request** — Safari can silently hand back a PNG when asked for WebP; `encodeCutout` checks the returned blob's actual type and only keeps WebP if it's genuinely WebP *and* smaller.
- **Never worse** — a flat cutout that would encode larger as WebP keeps its PNG.
- **The tagger accepts `image/webp`** — confirmed against the Anthropic vision docs (supported alongside jpeg/png/gif).

## Verified in real Chrome (not jsdom)

The one browser-specific risk is canvas WebP encoding. Ran the exact encode path against a transparent-alpha source:

| Check | Result |

- **170 tests** (was 164; +6 covering WebP success, the PNG fallbacks, size comparison, and a throwing encoder)
- `tsc --noEmit` clean · `npm run build` clean

## Scope

Only new uploads store WebP. Existing PNG cutouts are untouched — `displayPath()` reads whatever the row says, so the two coexist. A one-off backfill for existing items is a separate plan (`cutout-backfill`).

Confirmed the key constraint: **main has 5 pre-existing lint errors**, so CI must *not* gate on lint or nothing could ever merge. CI will run `test:run` + `tsc` + `build` (all green on main); lint stays out until those errors are cleaned up separately.

## What else we can add to the `main` ruleset

Beyond require-PR + CI + block-force-push/delete, two are worth adding, two are optional:

**Worth adding (I'll include these):**
- **Require branch up-to-date before merge** — pairs with CI: guarantees tests ran against the actual post-merge state, not a stale base. This is what catches "two PRs each green alone, broken together" — exactly the stacking risk we hit earlier.
- **Require conversation resolution** — all PR review threads resolved before merge. Low cost, and it matters once `/code-review` leaves comments.

**Optional (say the word):**
- **Require linear history** — no merge commits, forces squash/rebase. Cleaner history, but you currently use merge-commit PRs, so it'd change your merge button. I'd leave it off unless you want clean history.
- **Require signed commits** — GPG/SSH-signed. Real security value but adds setup friction; usually overkill for solo.

## Sequencing (to avoid blocking anything)

CI has to be on `main` *before* the ruleset requires it, or open PRs get stuck. So:
1. I create the CI workflow on its own branch → PR → CI runs and proves green
2. You merge that PR **and** #10 (webp) — no ruleset active yet, nothing blocked
3. *Then* I create the ruleset requiring the `CI` check

CI is green and the required check is named **`verify`** — that's the one string you'll need. Here's the full picture.

## What a ruleset is

A **ruleset** is GitHub's modern replacement for "branch protection rules." It's a named set of conditions that GitHub enforces on branches matching a pattern (here, `main`). Once active, it blocks any action that violates the rules — for everyone, including you — so nobody can accidentally force-push over `main`, delete it, or merge code that fails CI. It's the machine enforcing the discipline instead of relying on memory. (The lapse that put attribution in PR #9 is the same class of problem — a rule that depends on remembering. Rulesets make "don't merge broken code" impossible rather than merely discouraged.)

## Two ways to create it

**Option A — I do it via the API** (one command, guaranteed to match exactly what we designed). Fastest and no clicking.

**Option B — you do it in Settings.** Since you asked for the checkboxes, here's the exact path:

**Settings → Rules → Rulesets → New ruleset → New branch ruleset**

Then:

| Field | Set to |
|---|---|
| **Ruleset Name** | `main protection` |
| **Enforcement status** | **Active** |
| **Target branches** | Add target → **Include default branch** (that's `main`) |

Then tick these **Branch rules**:

- ☑️ **Restrict deletions**
- ☑️ **Block force pushes**
- ☑️ **Require a pull request before merging**
  - Required approvals: **0** (so you can still merge your own PRs)
  - ☑️ **Require conversation resolution before merging**
- ☑️ **Require status checks to pass**
  - ☑️ **Require branches to be up to date before merging**
  - Add checks → type **`verify`** → select it

Leave **Require linear history** and **Require signed commits** unchecked (the two optional ones we discussed).

Click **Create**.

## Important: order

Don't create it until **PR #11 (CI) and #10 (webp) are both merged to `main`**. The ruleset requires the `verify` check — if you enable it while those PRs are open, they'd get stuck (their branches predate CI). Merge both first (nothing blocks them yet), then create the ruleset.

**So the sequence is:** merge #10 → merge #11 → then create the ruleset (A or B).

Want me to just do **Option A** for you once you've merged #10 and #11? Say the word and it's one command. Or if you'd rather click through B yourself, the checklist above is complete.

content.text:
Here's the honest situation — and there's a real prerequisite problem, not just a checkbox.

## What Vercel preview deployments are

Once Vercel is connected to a GitHub repo, **every PR automatically gets its own deployed preview URL** plus a status check (just like `verify`). You can then require that check in the ruleset. It's the right tool for what you're describing.

## But two things are missing

**1. Vercel isn't connected at all.** No `.vercel`, no `vercel.json`, no Vercel checks on any PR. It's never been linked.

**2. The bigger blocker: there's no hosted backend.** Your `.env.local` points at a **local** Supabase stack (`127.0.0.1`). The app has only ever run against localhost. A Vercel preview lives on the public internet — it can't reach your laptop's Supabase. So a preview would *build* fine but be a **broken shell**: no login, no closet, no generation, because auth/DB/storage/AI all point nowhere.

That's the real work here. Connecting Vercel is 10 minutes; giving it something to talk to is the actual project.

## What each part needs — and who can do it

| Step | Who |
|---|---|
| Create a **hosted Supabase project** (EU, per the spec), push migrations to it | You (dashboard) — I can prep the migration/push commands |
| **Connect Vercel ↔ GitHub** (OAuth in the Vercel dashboard) | **You only** — I'm not permitted to do OAuth/account connections |
| Set env vars in Vercel (Supabase URL/key, `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, Google pair) | You paste them; I can document exactly which |
| Add preview/prod domains to **Google OAuth + Supabase redirect allowlist** | You (dashboards); I can give the exact URLs |
| A `vercel.json` if any build config is needed | Me |

## My honest recommendation

Two facts change the calculus:

- **Your `verify` CI already runs `npm run build`** — so build-breakage is *already* caught before merge. A Vercel preview's added value is the clickable, functioning URL — which needs the hosted backend to be worth anything.
- Standing up hosted Supabase + OAuth redirects is a genuine milestone (it's essentially "go live"), not a PR-hygiene tweak.

So I'd **not** bolt this onto the current cleanup work. I'd finish the daily-drop plans against local dev, then do "hosting" as its own focused piece — hosted Supabase, Vercel, env, OAuth redirects, and *then* preview-gating — all together, because they only make sense as a set.

I'm with you, and here's how I'm actually applying it — not just agreeing.

**What I do:** at each fork I take the option that won't need undoing, even when it's more work now. Concrete examples from today:

gh pr create --base main --head feat/signed-url-cache \
 --title "feat: cache signed URLs so the browser can reuse images" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## The problem

`signItemImages()` called `createSignedUrls` on every request, and Supabase mints a **new token every call** for the same file. So re-signing the same image yields a different URL — which the browser treats as a different image and re-downloads. Measured on the generator: switching occasion produced **3 of 3 identical files but 0 of 3 identical URLs**, so every view re-fetched everything.

This compounds badly with the daily-drop model, where the same persisted look is re-opened all day.

## The fix

A process-wide cache keyed on the full storage path holds `path → { url, expiresAt }`. Only paths without a comfortably-fresh entry are re-signed; the rest are answered from cache with the **same URL**. Same 1-hour lifetime, same security model — the change is that we stop regenerating a token we already hold.

- **Refresh margin** — an entry within 10 minutes of expiry is treated as stale and re-signed early, so a URL is never handed to the browser about to 404 mid-view. The ~50-minute window is where the URL stays byte-identical and the browser cache works.
- **Pruning** — `store` drops already-expired entries each call, so a long-running server process doesn't accumulate an entry per image per user forever.
- **Keyed on the full path** (which begins with the owner's user id), so entries can't collide across users. Caching is safe because a signed URL is a capability for one path the caller already reached through RLS to request — it grants nothing they couldn't mint a line later.

The policy is pure functions (`partition` / `store`) in `lib/storage/url-cache.ts`; `signed.ts` only wires them to a real clock and Map.

## Verified in the browser (the same measurement that exposed the bug)

| Metric | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Same file across a re-sign | 3/3 | 3/3 |
| **Same full URL** | **0/3** | **3/3** |
| Same token | 0/3 | 3/3 |

Same three files, now the same three URLs — the browser can reuse them instead of re-downloading. Combined with the WebP work (#10), a persisted daily look downloads once and costs nothing on re-view.

## Checks

- **177 tests** (was 170; +7 covering fresh reuse, the refresh margin, expiry, mixed batches, and pruning)
- `tsc --noEmit` clean · `npm run build` clean · no caller changes (signature unchanged)

## Scope

Per-server-instance cache — a different serverless lambda mints its own, which is fine: the win is per-session locality, not global dedup. A route proxy for *permanently* stable URLs is deferred to Phase 2, when share cards need it anyway.
EOF
)" 2>&1 | tail -2

content.text:
Really good question to ask *now* — Plan 4 isn't built, so rethinking it is free; rethinking it after would be the exact rework you told me to avoid. And I'll be honest even though this is my own proposal: **I think the mandatory morning question is not the best approach.** Let me show my work from both sides.

## Customer side

- **It's a gate in front of the magic moment.** The whole promise is "open the app, your looks are there." A question — even one tap — is a speed bump between the user and the payoff. And it's not a one-time onboarding cost; it's a **daily tax**, every morning, forever. CLAUDE.md says in bold: *"Don't gate the magic moment."* This gates it.
- **People don't reliably think in "occasions" at 7am.** Sometimes you know "today's a work day." Often you just want to *see outfits*. Making the user classify their day before anything appears is asking them to do the app's job.
- **Charming on day 1, annoying by day 30.** "Yes, work. Same as every weekday. Why do you keep asking."

## Our side

- **Every added step loses users.** For a *habit* product, morning friction is the single most likely thing to kill the daily habit you're trying to build. That's the worst place to add a tap.
- **Here's the thing that changes everything:** the cost saving and the question are **separable**. I conflated them when I proposed it. The cost win (4 AI calls → 1) comes from **lazy per-occasion generation** — generating only what's shown, and other occasions on first tap. That works *whether or not you ask a question*. The question adds friction; it does **not** add the cost saving. Lazy generation does that on its own.

So the question only buys one thing: intent accuracy (knowing it's a work day). And you can get *most* of that for free.

## The better approach

**Infer a smart default, show looks instantly, keep the chips.**

- Weekday → default to your work/everyday occasion (you already collect dress codes in onboarding). Saturday/Sunday → weekend. The calendar already knows the day; the weather's already known.
- Show that occasion's looks **immediately, no gate**.
- The occasion chips stay — so the user *states intent when they want to* by tapping, and that occasion lazily generates once, then caches.

This keeps **every** benefit — one AI call in the morning, lazy generation, the "styling your day" framing on the one call that runs — while removing the daily friction and honoring "don't gate the magic moment." It serves both the "just show me" user and the "let me choose" user. A mandatory question serves only the second.

## My recommendation

Revise Plan 4: **drop the "What's today?" screen; add day-of-week → occasion inference as the default; keep lazy per-occasion generation.** Same cost profile, strictly better UX.

One honest counterpoint, so I'm not overselling: if your users had *wildly* unpredictable days where a wrong default would waste their first impression, a question could earn its place. But even then, a smart default with a one-tap override beats a mandatory gate — so I can't find a case where asking-every-morning wins.

Want me to rewrite the Plan 4 spec around the smart-default approach before we build it? (I'll sync main from your merge of #12 either way.)

# Brainstorming Ideas Into Designs

Help turn ideas into fully formed designs and specs through natural collaborative dialogue.

Start by understanding the current project context, then ask questions one at a time to refine the idea. Once you understand what you're building, present the design and get user approval.

<HARD-GATE>
Do NOT invoke any implementation skill, write any code, scaffold any project, or take any implementation action until you have presented a design and the user has approved it. This applies to EVERY project regardless of perceived simplicity.
</HARD-GATE>

## Anti-Pattern: "This Is Too Simple To Need A Design"

Every project goes through this process. A todo list, a single-function utility, a config change — all of them. "Simple" projects are where unexamined assumptions cause the most wasted work. The design can be short (a few sentences for truly simple projects), but you MUST present it and get approval.

## Checklist

You MUST create a task for each of these items and complete them in order:

1. **Explore project context** — check files, docs, recent commits
2. **Offer the visual companion just-in-time** — NOT upfront. The first time a question would genuinely be clearer shown than described, offer it then (its own message); on approval its browser tab opens for you. If no visual question ever arises, never offer it. See the Visual Companion section below.
3. **Ask clarifying questions** — one at a time, understand purpose/constraints/success criteria
4. **Propose 2-3 approaches** — with trade-offs and your recommendation
5. **Present design** — in sections scaled to their complexity, get user approval after each section
6. **Write design doc** — save to `docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md` and commit
7. **Spec self-review** — quick inline check for placeholders, contradictions, ambiguity, scope (see below)
8. **User reviews written spec** — ask user to review the spec file before proceeding
9. **Transition to implementation** — invoke writing-plans skill to create implementation plan

## Process Flow

```dot

    "Explore project context" [shape=box];
    "Ask clarifying questions" [shape=box];
    "Propose 2-3 approaches" [shape=box];
    "Present design sections" [shape=box];
    "User approves design?" [shape=diamond];
    "Write design doc" [shape=box];
    "Spec self-review\n(fix inline)" [shape=box];
    "User reviews spec?" [shape=diamond];
    "Invoke writing-plans skill" [shape=doublecircle];

    "Explore project context" -> "Ask clarifying questions";
    "Ask clarifying questions" -> "Propose 2-3 approaches";
    "Propose 2-3 approaches" -> "Present design sections";
    "Present design sections" -> "User approves design?";
    "User approves design?" -> "Present design sections" [label="no, revise"];
    "User approves design?" -> "Write design doc" [label="yes"];
    "Write design doc" -> "Spec self-review\n(fix inline)";
    "Spec self-review\n(fix inline)" -> "User reviews spec?";
    "User reviews spec?" -> "Write design doc" [label="changes requested"];
    "User reviews spec?" -> "Invoke writing-plans skill" [label="approved"];
}
```

**The terminal state is invoking writing-plans.** Do NOT invoke frontend-design, mcp-builder, or any other implementation skill. The ONLY skill you invoke after brainstorming is writing-plans.

## The Process

**Understanding the idea:**

- Check out the current project state first (files, docs, recent commits)
- Before asking detailed questions, assess scope: if the request describes multiple independent subsystems (e.g., "build a platform with chat, file storage, billing, and analytics"), flag this immediately. Don't spend questions refining details of a project that needs to be decomposed first.
- If the project is too large for a single spec, help the user decompose into sub-projects: what are the independent pieces, how do they relate, what order should they be built? Then brainstorm the first sub-project through the normal design flow. Each sub-project gets its own spec → plan → implementation cycle.
- For appropriately-scoped projects, ask questions one at a time to refine the idea
- Prefer multiple choice questions when possible, but open-ended is fine too
- Only one question per message - if a topic needs more exploration, break it into multiple questions
- Focus on understanding: purpose, constraints, success criteria

**Exploring approaches:**

- Propose 2-3 different approaches with trade-offs
- Present options conversationally with your recommendation and reasoning
- Lead with your recommended option and explain why

**Presenting the design:**

- Once you believe you understand what you're building, present the design
- Scale each section to its complexity: a few sentences if straightforward, up to 200-300 words if nuanced
- Ask after each section whether it looks right so far
- Cover: architecture, components, data flow, error handling, testing
- Be ready to go back and clarify if something doesn't make sense

**Design for isolation and clarity:**

- Break the system into smaller units that each have one clear purpose, communicate through well-defined interfaces, and can be understood and tested independently
- For each unit, you should be able to answer: what does it do, how do you use it, and what does it depend on?
- Can someone understand what a unit does without reading its internals? Can you change the internals without breaking consumers? If not, the boundaries need work.
- Smaller, well-bounded units are also easier for you to work with - you reason better about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. When a file grows large, that's often a signal that it's doing too much.

**Working in existing codebases:**

- Explore the current structure before proposing changes. Follow existing patterns.
- Where existing code has problems that affect the work (e.g., a file that's grown too large, unclear boundaries, tangled responsibilities), include targeted improvements as part of the design - the way a good developer improves code they're working in.
- Don't propose unrelated refactoring. Stay focused on what serves the current goal.

## After the Design

**Documentation:**

- Write the validated design (spec) to `docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`
  - (User preferences for spec location override this default)
- Use elements-of-style:writing-clearly-and-concisely skill if available
- Commit the design document to git

**Spec Self-Review:**
After writing the spec document, look at it with fresh eyes:

1. **Placeholder scan:** Any "TBD", "TODO", incomplete sections, or vague requirements? Fix them.
2. **Internal consistency:** Do any sections contradict each other? Does the architecture match the feature descriptions?
3. **Scope check:** Is this focused enough for a single implementation plan, or does it need decomposition?
4. **Ambiguity check:** Could any requirement be interpreted two different ways? If so, pick one and make it explicit.

Fix any issues inline. No need to re-review — just fix and move on.

**User Review Gate:**
After the spec review loop passes, ask the user to review the written spec before proceeding:

> "Spec written and committed to `<path>`. Please review it and let me know if you want to make any changes before we start writing out the implementation plan."

Wait for the user's response. If they request changes, make them and re-run the spec review loop. Only proceed once the user approves.

**Implementation:**

- Invoke the writing-plans skill to create a detailed implementation plan
- Do NOT invoke any other skill. writing-plans is the next step.

## Key Principles

- **One question at a time** - Don't overwhelm with multiple questions
- **Multiple choice preferred** - Easier to answer than open-ended when possible
- **YAGNI ruthlessly** - Remove unnecessary features from all designs
- **Explore alternatives** - Always propose 2-3 approaches before settling
- **Incremental validation** - Present design, get approval before moving on
- **Be flexible** - Go back and clarify when something doesn't make sense

## Visual Companion

A browser-based companion for showing mockups, diagrams, and visual options during brainstorming. Available as a tool — not a mode. Accepting the companion means it's available for questions that benefit from visual treatment; it does NOT mean every question goes through the browser.

**Offering the companion (just-in-time):** Do NOT offer it upfront. Wait until a question would genuinely be clearer shown than told — a real mockup / layout / diagram question, not merely a UI *topic*. The first time that happens, offer it then, as its own message:
> "This next part might be easier if I show you — I can put together mockups, diagrams, and comparisons in a browser tab as we go. It's still new and can be token-intensive. Want me to? I'll open it for you."

**This offer MUST be its own message.** Only the offer — no clarifying question, summary, or other content. Wait for the user's response. If they accept, start the server with `--open` so their browser opens to the first screen automatically. If they decline, continue text-only and don't offer again unless they raise it.

**Per-question decision:** Even after the user accepts, decide FOR EACH QUESTION whether to use the browser or the terminal. The test: **would the user understand this better by seeing it than reading it?**

- **Use the browser** for content that IS visual — mockups, wireframes, layout comparisons, architecture diagrams, side-by-side visual designs
- **Use the terminal** for content that is text — requirements questions, conceptual choices, tradeoff lists, A/B/C/D text options, scope decisions

A question about a UI topic is not automatically a visual question. "What does personality mean in this context?" is a conceptual question — use the terminal. "Which wizard layout works better?" is a visual question — use the browser.

If they agree to the companion, read the detailed guide before proceeding:
`skills/brainstorming/visual-companion.md`

content.text:
Then let me think about this properly — as a product, both sides, optimizing for the *best* version, not the cheapest. This is worth doing well because the architecture we choose now determines whether we can grow it without tearing it up later.

## Reframe: the default isn't a rule, it's a *prediction of your day*

The weak version of this feature is "pick by day of week." The strong version is: **the app predicts what you're doing today and gets more right the more you use it.** That framing changes everything — because a *rule* is static, but a *prediction* can improve, and improvement-over-time is exactly what builds a habit and justifies a subscription.

## The signal ladder (cheap/static → rich/personal)

| Signal | What it tells us | Cost | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Day of week** | work-ish vs weekend-ish | free | weak alone (WFH, shift work, holidays break it) |
| **Onboarding occasions** | which occasions you dress for *at all* | free, already stored | strong *filter* — never open you on Evening if you don't dress for evenings |
| **Behavioral: your overrides** | your *actual* rhythm | small storage | **the real prize** — see below |
| **Real calendar** | literally what you're doing today | high (OAuth + privacy) | powerful but probably not worth it — see below |

## The prize is the override

Here's the insight that serves both sides: **every time the user corrects the default, that's the most valuable signal in the app.** "Defaulted to Work, they switched to Everyday" — do that three Mondays running and the app *knows* this person doesn't dress up for work, better than any rule could.

- **For the user:** the app stops being wrong. It learns *their* week, not a generic one. That's the feeling of an app that knows you.
- **For us:** it's a retention moat (the longer you use it, the better it fits, the harder to leave) *and* a paid-tier story ("Fitcheck learns your week"). It's a data flywheel that a competitor starting fresh can't copy.

## The one move that's genuinely future-proof (and nearly free now)

Even if we don't *build the learner* yet: **start logging the override signal from day 1.** When someone changes occasion away from the default, record it. We don't have to act on it immediately — but if we *don't* capture it now, then the day we build the learner we start from zero and have to wait months for data. Capturing it early is impossible to backfill and costs almost nothing. That's the "decide right so we never refactor" move applied here.

So the architecture is a single `predictOccasion(context)` where context grows over time — `{ date, occasions }` now, `+ history` later — additively, never a rewrite.

## On the calendar (the tempting "best signal")

I'll be honest rather than hype it: reading someone's real calendar *is* the theoretically best signal, but for a wardrobe app it's a **bad trade**. "Give a fashion app your calendar" is a hard trust ask, it's a GDPR liability (and CLAUDE.md makes GDPR a *marketing asset* — mishandling calendar data is the opposite of that), and events are messy to map ("Sync" vs "Dinner with Sarah" needs NLP). Behavioral learning gets you ~80% of the personalization with *none* of the privacy weight. I'd name it as a someday-maybe and not build toward it.

## And how it looks — make the intelligence legible

A smart default that's *silent* just feels like a random default — the user never perceives the smartness. So the app should say *why*, quietly: a one-line label above the looks —

> *"Styled for your Tuesday"* · or once it's learned · *"Your usual weekday look"*

This does two jobs: it makes the app feel like it knows you, and it makes correction feel natural ("no — weekend today") which *feeds the flywheel*. Silent-but-smart wastes the smartness.

---

So my recommended best-for-both shape: **rule + onboarding foundation (works day 1, legible "why"), log overrides from day 1, build the learner as the flywheel, skip the calendar.** One decision to land before I spec it:

content.text:
Two things there — let me take both, because the second one is a genuinely good catch that actually *simplifies* the whole design.

## On building the learner now — my honest take

Here's the one technical truth that decides this: **the learner cannot behave any differently from the rule until override data exists.** On day 1–14 there's no history to learn from, so a learner built today just falls through to the rule anyway. So building it now vs. building it in three weeks makes **zero difference to any user** until the data accrues.

What that means:

- Shipping the learner "now" doesn't make it *work* sooner — it can't, there's nothing to learn from yet.
- The thing that genuinely must exist now is the **seam + the override logging**. If we log overrides from day 1, the learner has months of real data waiting whenever we add it.
- And there's a quality cost to building it blind: the learning *rule* (how many overrides before it adapts? per-weekday or global? does old behavior decay?) is much better designed once you've *seen* real override patterns. Build it in a vacuum and you'll likely re-tune it against reality later — which is the rework you told me to avoid.

So my honest recommendation isn't "do less to save work" — it's: **ship the foundation + legible "why" + override logging now** (that's the whole valuable, shippable thing), and add the learner the moment there's data to design it against. You lose *nothing* user-facing by sequencing it that way, and you get a *better* learner. If you'd still rather have the full loop deployed and waiting, that's defensible — just know week 1 looks identical either way.

## On "what if they didn't pick Evening but later need it" — great catch, and it's already solved

This is the important realization: **all four occasion chips are always visible and tappable today.** `profiles.occasions` does *not* gate which chips appear — Everyday / Work / Weekend / Evening are always there. So someone who skipped Evening in onboarding can just *tap Evening any morning* and it generates on demand. No lockout, no settings screen needed for access.

That cleanly resolves the tension: **onboarding `occasions` becomes a soft signal that only seeds the smart default — it never locks anything.**

- Didn't pick Evening → we just won't *default* you to it. But it's one tap away, always.
- The chip you tap generates lazily and caches for the day, exactly like the others.

The only thing settings would add is letting someone *change their default preferences* after a life change (got a job → now dress for Work) so the *prediction* adapts. That's a nice profile-screen addition (the roadmap already has a profile hub, Plan 11) — but it's optional polish, not required, because access is never blocked.

---

So the design converges to something clean:

- `predictOccasion({ date, occasions })` → seeds the default each morning, respecting what they dress for, never picking an occasion they skipped
- A legible one-line "why" above the looks
- All four chips stay always-tappable (no lockout — your Evening concern handled by design, not a settings patch)
- **Log every override from day 1** — the flywheel's fuel, banked whether or not we build the learner yet
- Learner + profile-editable preferences = clean later additions, no rewrite

Before I write the spec, one thing to pin down so I build the right thing:

All approved — so we ship the smart default now and only *collect* override data for the future learner, no learner yet. Here's exactly what we'll build in place of the morning question.

## What ships — function by function

input.content:
# Smart Default Occasion — Design

_2026-07-23. Replaces the "What's today?" morning question with an inferred default. Local-only doc (docs/ is gitignored, per the project's meta-docs convention)._

## Problem

A daily-drop app must reach looks with zero friction ("Don't gate the magic moment", CLAUDE.md). An earlier idea — a mandatory morning "What's today?" question — was rejected: it's a daily tax between the user and the payoff, and it doesn't even earn the cost saving (lazy per-occasion generation, already shipped in the daily-looks work, delivers that regardless).

Instead, the app should **predict** the occasion the user most likely wants each morning, show it immediately, and get more right over time.

## Principles

- **The default is a prediction of your day, not a static rule.** A rule is fixed; a prediction can improve, and improvement-with-use is what builds a habit and justifies a subscription.
- **Make the intelligence legible.** A smart default shown *silently* just feels like a random default. A one-line "why" makes the app feel like it knows you, and makes correcting it feel natural — which feeds the flywheel.
- **The override is the prize.** Every time the user corrects the default, that's the highest-value signal in the app — their *actual* rhythm, better than any rule. We bank it from day 1.
- **Nothing is ever locked.** All four occasion chips stay tappable. Onboarding `occasions` is a *soft signal* that seeds the default; it never gates access.

## Signals considered

| Signal | Role | Decision |
|---|---|---|
| Day of week | weekday vs weekend | Used |
| Onboarding `occasions` (`profiles.occasions text[]`) | which occasions the user dresses for at all | Used — soft filter for the default |
| Override history | the user's real rhythm | **Logged now, consumed by the future learner** |
| Real calendar (Google) | literally what you're doing today | **Rejected.** Theoretically the best signal, but a bad trade for a wardrobe app: a hard trust ask, a GDPR liability (CLAUDE.md makes GDPR a marketing asset), and messy event→occasion mapping. Behavioral learning gets ~80% of the value with none of the privacy weight. |

## What ships now

### 1. Predictor — `lib/outfits/predict-occasion.ts` (pure, unit-tested)

```ts
predictOccasion(now: Date, timeZone: string, occasions: string[]): UiOccasion
```
- Day-of-week in the user's timezone (same `Intl` approach as `localDateFor`).
- **Weekday (Mon–Fri):** first available of `[Work, Everyday, Weekend, Evening]` present in `occasions`.
- **Weekend (Sat–Sun):** first available of `[Weekend, Everyday, Work, Evening]`.
- Empty/missing `occasions` → `everyday` (today's behavior — no regression).
- Never returns an occasion the user didn't select; but every chip stays tappable, so nothing is locked.

```ts
defaultReason(occasion: UiOccasion): string
```
- `work → "Styled for your work day"` · `everyday → "Everyday ease"` · `weekend → "Weekend, off-duty"` · `evening → "Out tonight"`. Copy tunable.

### 2. Server actions — `app/generate/actions.ts`

```ts
predictDefaultOccasion(): Promise<{ occasion: UiOccasion; reason: string }>
```
- One profile read (`occasions` + `location_timezone`) + date math. **No AI, no weather.** Called once on mount so the client seeds the right occasion before the first generate.
- If `location_timezone` is null (never resolved), fall back to UTC — the default is soft.

```ts
logOccasionOverride(input: { predicted: UiOccasion; chosen: UiOccasion }): Promise<void>
```
- Fire-and-forget. Writes one row to `occasion_overrides`. Never blocks the UI. Only called when `chosen !== predicted`.

### 3. Migration — `occasion_overrides`

```sql
create table public.occasion_overrides (
  id            uuid primary key default gen_random_uuid(),
  user_id       uuid not null references public.profiles(id) on delete cascade,
  generated_on  date not null,          -- user's LOCAL date (day-of-week derivable)
  predicted     text not null,
  chosen        text not null,
  created_at    timestamptz default now()
);
```
Flat RLS (`user_id = auth.uid()`), append-only. **Unused by any logic today** — purely banks the flywheel signal so the future learner starts with real history instead of zero. Impossible to backfill, so it must exist from day 1.

### 4. Client — `components/generate/stylist.tsx`

- Replace the hardcoded `useState<UiOccasion>("everyday")` seed: on mount, call `predictDefaultOccasion`, set `occasion` and `reason`.
- When a chip tap sets an occasion `!== predicted`, fire `logOccasionOverride(predicted, chosen)` (fire-and-forget).
- Pass `reason` down.

### 5. View — `components/generate/stylist-view.tsx`

- A quiet one-line label above the looks (design-system toned) showing the active occasion's phrase. Reads as the "why" on the default; as a caption after an override.

## Non-goals (now)

- **The learner** — not built; only the seam and data. See below.
- **Weather-drift "restyle" offer** — separate concern, its own later spec.
- **Editing occasions after onboarding** — access is never blocked (chips always visible), so this is optional polish. A future profile-screen (roadmap Plan 11) can let a user update `profiles.occasions` so the *default* adapts to a life change (e.g. got a job). Not required here.
- **Real calendar integration** — rejected, see Signals.

## Future: the learner

_Not built now. Documented so the seam and data we ship are shaped correctly, and so the design is ready when usage data exists._

**Why later, not now:** the learner cannot behave differently from the rule until override history exists — on day 1 it falls through to `predictOccasion` anyway. Worse, its learning *rule* (below) is best designed after seeing real override patterns; building it blind risks tuning it twice. So we ship the rule + capture data now, and add the learner when the data can inform its design. Users see identical behavior in week 1 either way.

**What it reads:** `occasion_overrides`, aggregated per user. Day-of-week is derivable from `generated_on`. The learner asks, per user: *"On this kind of day (weekday/weekend, or per-weekday), which occasion do they actually settle on?"*

**The seam:** `predictOccasion` gains a third input without changing its callers' shape —
```ts
predictOccasion(now, timeZone, occasions, history?)  // history optional; absent → today's rule
```
When `history` is supplied and shows a stable pattern (e.g. ≥ N overrides to the same occasion on the same day-type), it overrides the rule's pick. Absent or below threshold → the rule stands. This is additive: the current pure function and its tests keep passing; the learner is a new branch inside it plus a `loadOverrideHistory()` reader.

**Learning-rule sketch (to be tuned against real data):**
- Scope: per weekday (Mon…Sun) is richer than weekday/weekend, but needs more data — start weekday/weekend, refine if signal supports finer grain.
- Threshold: require a minimum count and a clear majority before adapting, so one-off overrides don't move the default.
- Recency: weight recent overrides more (life changes); optionally decay old ones.
- Legibility carries over: the "why" label becomes *"Your usual weekday look"* once learned — the app visibly gets more personal.

**Business rationale (why this is worth the flywheel):** a default that gets *right* builds the daily habit; a default that stays *wrong* makes the user override every morning → friction → churn. The override history is a retention moat (the app fits better the longer you use it, which a fresh competitor can't copy) and a natural paid-tier story ("Fitcheck learns your week"). Capturing the signal now, for near-zero cost, is what makes that future cheap.

## Testing

- `predict-occasion.test.ts`: weekday→Work when dressed for it; weekday→Everyday when not; weekend→Weekend; empty occasions→everyday; never returns an unselected occasion; timezone affects the day boundary; reason copy per occasion.
- `occasion_overrides` migration applies; a logged override lands with the local date.
- Client: mount seeds the predicted occasion; an override fires the log; a same-as-default tap does not.
- Verify in the iOS Simulator: correct default per day, legible label, override still one tap, override row written.
